idiom_name: distinct principals per step + persisted two-step workflow, checked at the enforcement point
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: split the operation into steps whose authorities are mutually insufficient, give each step its own authenticated principal (account, role, service identity, process uid), and persist the workflow's intermediate state (initiated_by, reviewed revision, approved_by) so the terminal transition can require a recorded second principal. The distinctness predicate - acting principal != initiator - belongs at the enforcement point on every path, not in the UI and not in a client-supplied field, and the check plus the state transition must be one atomic step (transaction, conditional write, lock) so two approvals cannot race and a stale approval cannot be reused after an edit. Where the boundary must survive code in the same address space, or the same trust domain, move the second duty into a separate process, account or service and authenticate the caller's identity at that boundary (peer credentials, tokens) rather than trusting in-process role conventions.
code_sketch:
request = workflow.create(operation, initiated_by=alice)   # durable pending state
request = review(request, revision=request.revision)       # exactly what the approver saw
assert actor != request.initiated_by                       # at the enforcement point, every path
workflow.commit(request, approved_by=actor)                # atomic; requires the distinct actor
pitfalls: Recording the approval without checking the principal, or checking a client-supplied identity, leaves the workflow with two logged steps and one effective actor.
A read-compare-write transition lets two approvers both observe 'pending', or lets an approval survive an edit; the distinctness check and the state change must be atomic and bound to a revision.
Duties that are separated in policy but recombined in deployment (one account for both steps, one admin able to grant the missing half) turn the rule into documentation.

Wrong move: define the split as a role pair but let provisioning hand out composite or derived roles -> one grantee quietly accumulates maker and checker rights inside a bundle role while every per-role check still passes -> test the forbidden duty pairs against effective permissions at assignment time and in periodic access reviews, not just against the role definitions.

Wrong move: verify the distinct-principal predicate at approval time but execute the change under a shared executor or pipeline identity -> whoever can trigger execution runs any pre-approved work and the enforcement point never sees the real actor -> bind the terminal transition to the authenticated executor as well, giving maker, checker and executor flows their own service identities with different owners.
